_comment: What each measure is CALLED on a diagram, in two fields and a template.
WHY NOT THE ID. The diagram used to label its measure nodes `cbam:FIN-03`. That is
the right thing to store and the wrong thing to draw: the id is how the register, the
graph and the gates refer to a measure, and it tells a reader nothing about what the
measure does. The id has not gone anywhere — it is in the hover detail and it is the
heading of the measure's own page — but the node now says what it is.
WHY NOT A LABEL FIELD. A free label per measure would drift: twenty sectors written
months apart, each phrasing its own nodes, and no two diagrams reading alike. So the
label is COMPUTED from two fields by one template in sources/sector_map.py:
object      the thing the measure acts on, as a noun phrase
instrument  the legal device it acts with, from the closed list in sector_map.py
short_label = object                 where instrument is null
= object + ' ' + instrument   otherwise
`instrument` is null where the object already names the device — 'CBAM certificates'
is the instrument, and 'CBAM certificates obligation' is the same fact said twice and
four characters over the limit. Null is therefore allowed and is not a gap.
THE GATES (sources/check_sector_schema.py): every measure in a sector view has an
entry; every instrument is in the vocabulary; every computed label is at most 26
characters, is unique within the sector's diagram, and carries no word from
sources/display_vocabulary.py.
Keyed by the register id, `<file>:<id>`, so an entry cannot name a measure that does
not exist. Entries are shared across sectors: a measure keeps its label everywhere.
THE PLAIN BLOCK (brief 4 §5). The diagram label says what a measure is ABOUT in 26
characters. The sector page's key-measures list has to say what it REQUIRES OR
GRANTS, to somebody who has never read the act, in a title and one sentence — and
neither can be computed from `object` and `instrument`, because neither of those
fields knows whether the measure obliges, permits or pays.
title     what it requires or grants. Never the act's name, never its article,
no numbers: the numbers are in the sentence, where they can carry a
date.
sentence  one sentence, no jargon, with every FIGURE in a {slot} that
sources/build_importance.py fills from the measure's own money block.
WHY THE SLOTS. An authored sentence with a number typed into it is a number nobody
gated, and it rots the day the carbon price moves. The slots are the same discipline
the perimeter paragraph uses in data/prose.json: the words are written once and
reviewed, the figures are computed on every build. A slot that cannot be filled for
the measure it is written on fails the build rather than rendering a blank.
{money_per_tonne}  the per-tonne figure, e.g. '€75.46 per tonne'
{money_annual}     the annual total, e.g. '€990 million a year'
{money_awarded}    money awarded to date, e.g. '€381 million'
WHERE THE PLAIN BLOCK LIVES, AND WHY IT IS NOT ALWAYS SHARED. `object` and
`instrument` are shared across sectors and always will be: they name the legal device,
which does not change when a second industry is reached. The plain block does change,
because it names the PRODUCT — and a measure page for steel that said "per tonne of
clinker" would be the cement dataset talking on somebody else's page.
So there are two slots and the reader is resolved per sector:
plain_by_sector.<slug>   the sector's own wording, consulted first
plain                    the shared block, used only where the measure's wording
is genuinely product-free — governance, verification,
procedural and infrastructure measures read the same
everywhere and are written once
A SHARED BLOCK MAY NOT NAME ANY SECTOR'S PRODUCT. That is the rule that stops the
fallback from becoming a trap: a shared block still saying "clinker" would render
cement's sentence on the third sector the day a measure reaches it, and nobody would
be told. The gate holds every shared block against every sector's product vocabulary
and fails on a hit, so the wrong sentence is a build error rather than a page nobody
re-read. A measure that reaches a sector and resolves to neither slot fails the same
way.
THE GATES (sources/check_sector_schema.py): every measure that reaches a mapped sector
resolves to a plain block; no shared block names a product; no per-sector block names
another sector's product; the title carries no digits and no word from
sources/display_vocabulary.py; the sentence is one sentence, names only known slots,
and any bare number in it appears in the measure's own `when` field — which is how a
date is allowed to be written out and a euro figure is not.
A SENTENCE NEVER ASKS FOR A NUMBER THE PLATFORM CANNOT COMPUTE. cbam:FIN-03 is the
live case: its cement block states the certificate cost from the money model, and the
steel block states the obligation qualitatively because no certificate model exists
for steel yet. An unfillable slot is a build failure by design, and writing round it
is what a reviewer does instead of loosening the rule.

cement.title: Importers pay for the carbon in the cement they bring in
cement.sentence: The carbon in imported cement is charged at {money_per_tonne} at today's carbon price, and from 2028 the certificates covering it have to be bought in the same year they are used.

steel.title: Importers pay for the carbon in the steel they bring in
steel.sentence: Importers of steel have to buy certificates covering the carbon emitted making it, and from 2028 those certificates have to be bought in the same year they are used.

plain.title: Europe sets itself capacity goals for its own raw materials
plain.sentence: By 2030 the Union is to be able to extract, process and recycle set shares of the strategic raw materials it consumes each year, rather than buying all of them from outside.

plain.title: No single country may supply most of a strategic material
plain.sentence: By 2030 the Union's yearly consumption of each strategic raw material is to come from several countries, with no one of them above the share the act sets.

plain.title: Raw material projects can apply for strategic status
plain.sentence: A raw materials project can apply to be recognised as strategic, which brings faster permitting and easier access to finance, by filing evidence against the criteria together with a business plan, a timetable and environmental and consultation plans.

cement.title: Free carbon allowances for European kilns are being withdrawn
cement.sentence: European cement makers lose their free allowances on a fixed schedule that reaches zero in 2038, which costs {money_per_tonne} of clinker at today's carbon price and more every year after that.

steel.title: Free carbon allowances for European steel are being withdrawn
steel.sentence: European steel makers lose their free allowances on a fixed schedule that reaches zero in 2038, which costs {money_per_tonne} of hot metal at today's carbon price and more every year after that.

cement.title: EU grants for cutting industrial emissions
cement.sentence: {money_awarded} has been awarded from the Innovation Fund to European cement projects that capture their CO2.

steel.title: EU grants for making iron without coal
steel.sentence: {money_awarded} has been awarded from the Innovation Fund to European steel projects that reduce iron ore without coal.

batsol.title: EU grants for building battery factories
batsol.sentence: The Innovation Fund, financed by auctioning carbon allowances, has awarded grants to European cell works through its first battery call, and published no figure for what any one of them received.

batsol.title: Carmakers pay for every gram they are over their target
batsol.sentence: A carmaker whose fleet exceeds its target pays a premium for each gram per kilometre of the excess on every vehicle it registered, which is what makes the target a purchasing decision rather than an ambition.

batsol.title: Carmakers must halve the emissions of the cars they sell
batsol.sentence: From 2030 the average new car sold in the Union has to cut its emissions by more than half against the baseline year, with new vans close behind, which is the demand a factory being built today supplies.

batsol.title: New cars sold in Europe have to be zero-emission
batsol.sentence: From 2035 a new passenger car sold in the Union may emit no CO2 where it is driven, which at fleet scale means the car carries a battery.

plain.title: A low-carbon claim has to be checked by an accredited verifier
plain.sentence: Before a product can be called low-carbon, the emissions figures behind the claim have to be verified by an accredited verifier.

cement.title: Public contracts must buy low-carbon concrete
cement.sentence: From 2029, public buyers have to require concrete that meets the low-carbon and Union-origin rules the act sets, in the contracts the act covers.

steel.title: Public contracts must buy low-carbon steel
steel.sentence: From 2029, public buyers have to require steel that meets the low-carbon and Union-origin rules the act sets, in the contracts the act covers.

steel.title: A quarter of the steel in public projects must be low-carbon
steel.sentence: From 2029, at least a quarter of the steel used in the buildings, infrastructure and vehicles the act covers has to be low-carbon steel.

plain.title: Public support schemes must favour low-carbon materials
plain.sentence: From 2029, public schemes that pay for construction have to be built around the same low-carbon and Union-origin requirements as public contracts.

batsol.title: Public contracts for battery storage must buy European
batsol.sentence: Public buyers procuring battery storage have to apply the Union-origin requirements the act sets out for it, so part of the demand is closed to a cell made elsewhere.

batsol.title: Public schemes may only subsidise European-made electric cars
batsol.sentence: A public scheme that pays towards buying or leasing a new electric vehicle may only cover vehicles meeting the Union-origin requirements, which reaches the battery through the car it sits in.

plain.title: Oil and gas producers must provide somewhere to put the CO2
plain.sentence: Europe's oil and gas producers have to open, between them, enough permanent CO2 storage to meet the Union's target for 2030, each taking a share in proportion to what it produces.

plain.title: CO2 pipelines and stores must be open to whoever needs them
plain.sentence: Whoever owns a CO2 pipeline or a storage site has to let others use it on fair and open terms, so that a capture project is not stopped by the party that owns the route to the ground.

plain.title: Purchase subsidies have to favour a resilient supply
plain.sentence: A scheme that subsidises buying clean technology has to be designed so that products with a high sustainability and resilience contribution either receive more money or are the only ones eligible.

plain.title: Faster permits for projects recognised as strategic
plain.sentence: A project can apply to be recognised as strategic, which shortens its permitting, by filing evidence against the criteria together with a business plan and a financing outline.
